narrative: The model estimated a 58.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that risk estimate was high enough to lead to rejection, your law school application was denied. This is a probability, not a certainty, but it means the model saw a somewhat higher-than-half chance of failure. The prediction was driven mainly by three factors, ranked by influence. Your LSAT score was the most important factor and the only one of the top three that pushed toward failure: at 22.5 it is well below the 37.18 average among accepted students. The second factor, your undergraduate GPA, pushed slightly toward passing even though your 2.90 is below the accepted average of 3.23. The third factor, family income, also pushed slightly toward passing; your middle-income background is common among accepted students, about 34.8%. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction. The strong LSAT concern outweighed the modest favorable effects of GPA and family income. To improve your position, focus first on the LSAT: consider a structured retake plan and a score goal above the accepted average. Ask an admissions advisor how to contextualize your GPA and academic record, and whether additional coursework or a revised personal statement can strengthen a future application. Reapply only after addressing the LSAT weakness and documenting any academic improvement or circumstances.
